The current test will also examine what happens to the chips under heat and space radiation. Radiation can alter stored data in ways that ordinary monitoring tools may miss. Google’s tests on Earth suggested inference workloads would be relatively resilient, and the satellite will let the team check that finding in space.

Google’s longer-term plan calls for satellites to share large workloads over high-speed optical links. If the prototype’s chips perform well, two satellites planned for 2027 will test those links and carry higher-power systems.</linkedin_post>

<constraints>
- Return plain prose without hashtags, emojis, decorative symbols, headings, bold text, bullet points or numbered lists.
- Avoid successive isolated one-sentence paragraphs and sequences of clipped sentences or fragments used for drama. An occasional short sentence is fine when it serves the point.
- State claims directly. Avoid rhetorical reframing such as "This isn't X; it's Y," "X, not Y," and "not X, but Y." Keep necessary factual distinctions.
- State additional capabilities directly, without "not just X," "not only X" or "more than just X" constructions.
- Omit interchangeable slogans, generic scene-setting, teaser questions and labels announcing an insight, such as "Here's the thing," "The real story," or "The takeaway?" Start with the substance.
- Replace generic benefit claims and inflated significance with the actual change or consequence. Avoid promises to "unlock potential," "transform everything" or "change the game."
- Use plain words and direct verbs. Avoid prestige vocabulary, corporate jargon and noun-heavy phrases when ordinary wording says the same thing.
- Connect ideas through their actual relationship. Avoid stock pivots such as "But here's the catch," "Let that sink in," or "And that's where things get interesting."
- Avoid invented objections, staged revelations and claims that a point is "honest," "uncomfortable" or "what nobody is talking about."
- Do not force ideas into groups of three, matching sentence templates, decorative "from X to Y" ranges or repeated short payoff lines. Let the content determine the rhythm.
- Avoid trailing significance clauses such as ", highlighting the importance of..." or ", underscoring the need for..." State a useful point directly or omit it.
- Keep uncertainty where it is needed, without stacked hedges, repeated qualifications or intensifiers added for emphasis.
- Avoid recap endings, universal lessons, generic predictions and requests for reactions such as "Thoughts?" or "Agree?" Stop when the post has said what it needs to say.
- Do not invent personal experiences, testing, conversations, emotions or discovery stories for the person publishing the post.
- Avoid repeated em dashes, ellipses, exclamation marks or rhetorical questions used to manufacture suspense or emphasis.
</constraints>

Google’s Suncatcher prototype is running an AI model in orbit, with four TPUs aboard a satellite that generates up to 1 kW of power. For now, it can operate one chip at a time for about 20 minutes.

The first prompts included a request for a space-themed haiku. The more consequential tests will examine how the chips handle heat and radiation. Radiation can flip bits in memory and corrupt data without setting off typical monitoring tools. Ground tests suggested inference workloads would be less affected than model training, and the satellite gives Google a chance to test that in orbit.

If the prototype performs well, Google plans to launch two more satellites in 2027 with higher power generation and optical links between them. Those links are central to its plan for satellites to share large computing workloads.

The longer-term economics also depend on launch costs. Suncatcher researchers estimate that SpaceX would need 1,800 Starship flights to achieve the same learning-driven cost reductions it saw with earlier vehicles.

Google’s first data center satellite is operating in orbit, giving the company a chance to test how its AI chips respond to space radiation and thermal stress.

The satellite carries four TPUs, though its power supply allows it to run only one at a time for about 20 minutes. Engineers have prompted the onboard Gemma model to write poetry and report on conditions around the spacecraft.

Radiation can flip bits in memory, potentially corrupting data without triggering normal monitoring tools. Google’s ground tests suggested the effects would be limited for inference, the process of running an existing model. The orbital tests will show how the hardware performs under actual space conditions.

If the chips prove capable, Google plans to launch two higher-power satellites in 2027 and test optical links between them. Those links would let satellites share processing work, an approach Google hopes to use for larger workloads in orbit. </linkedin_post>
